only getting n_eff=2, your chains aren't converging. So you
might want to inspect how they're getting stuck.

Thanks very much for your response.

My R code implemented Euler's method to solve the ODE (actually a
version with "white noise" but the noise is very small in my example). I
solved the same equation in Stan and got reasonably similar results. I
assume Stan uses RK4? Although maybe it should use a symplectic
integrator ;-)

The initial value is the initial value for the simulation.

I can't explain it but the inference is now working both for simulations
generated by Stan and for simulations generated by my R code. It's
possibly because I am not very used to imperative languages and assume
when I calculate something then all the dependencies get re-calculated.
Of course I thought I had selected the whole region (in emacs) and
recalculated but maybe I was missing something.

Yes I noticed n_eff=2 wasn't good but thanks for pointing it out.

For future reference, how would one inspect how a chain is getting stuck?

For info, I was using Stan to confirm that my Sequential Monte Carlo
inference was giving sensible answers; it seems that it does.

Thanks once more to everyone who responded. I hope to write up the
example so it might be of some use to other Stan users.

Dominic.

Stan does use a symplectic integrator for the Hamiltonian simulation.
We're using a 5th-order Runge-Kutta from Boost for Stan's language and
we're about to add a stiff solver from CVODE (can't recall the algorithm
it uses).

If you're working in RStan, I believe the pairs plot will point
out where things go wrong. You can also inspect the divergences
directly --- they'll be 1 or 0, depending on whether there was
or wasn't an arithmetic issue. There's some fiddling to get them
out of the fit object. You can also look at the traceplots,
where a chain getting stuck for a long time will show up as a straight
line.

- Bob

forthcoming Riemannian HMC. It's based on Michael Betancourt's
arXiv papers (SoftAbs for defining a well-conditioned metric
based on a Hessian; Geometric no-U-turn sampler to deal with

I think it's more a matter of what tools are in your
toolbox. But there's been a lot of geometric analysis of
stats, not just for MCMC.

There's a nice survey of (Euclidean) HMC by Radford Neal in the
Handbook of MCMC (it's a free sample chapter).

The original Riemannian HMC paper is Girolami and Calderhead (Royal
Stats Society B), but I prefer the way Michael presents
it here:

http://arxiv.org/abs/1212.4693

and in a more general way, without the concrete smoothing proposal
for RHMC, here:

http://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.5110.pdf

There's a citation to the original paper RHMC paper in these if
want to track it down. Then there's the NUTS paper
for (Euclidean) HMC by Hoffman and Gelman (JMLR) and
Michael's generalization to RHMC (arXiv).

- Bob
